title: Routing a Local AI Farm Without Losing Conversation Truth
summary: Build a synchronous Express gateway that survives retries, streaming failures, replica changes, and explicit local-to-cloud switches while PostgreSQL remains the authority for every conversation.
learningObjectives: Separate load balancing, inference locality, identity, and durable conversation state.
Implement idempotent turn reservation with revisions and bounded leases.
Explain what streaming clients can recover after interruption and what they cannot.
Defend explicit cloud consent, bounded admission, and honest terminal statuses.

sections.title: 1. Define truth before choosing a router
paragraphs: Imagine two employees chatting while Nginx distributes HTTP connections across api1 and api2. Either Express process can fail between two messages. Behind them, inference A and inference B run the same Qwen weights, tokenizer, and chat template. The central question is not which process remembers the user. It is which component has authority to decide what the conversation contains. In this design, that authority is PostgreSQL. Express authenticates requests, checks ownership, commits turns, selects a provider, and records outcomes. Inference servers receive a constructed prompt and return generated text; their temporary caches are disposable.

Four identities must remain separate. A session identifies an authenticated principal. A conversation identifies an ordered history owned by that principal. A request ID identifies one attempted user turn. An inference node identifies a compute placement. Conflating these creates subtle failures: routing by a cookie does not enforce ownership, an HTTP connection is not a durable turn, and a warm prefix cache is not a history database. Keep secrets out of placement keys and logs. A random conversation identifier is a suitable locality key only after authorization has established that the caller owns it.

The downloadable reference is an educational Linux Docker scaffold, separate from this Windows-hosted learning application. It contains actual Express, PostgreSQL, and browser code rather than an architectural sketch. Start with the deployment article and [download the example bundle](/examples/ai-farm.zip). Inspect api/server.js and api/schema.sql before starting services. No inference server or model download was performed to produce this guide. The bundled client deliberately uses the gateway: llama.cpp's built-in chat interface talks directly to inference and therefore bypasses this application's authentication and durable history contract.

sections.title: 2. Authenticate the caller, then authorize the conversation
paragraphs: The example login accepts Admin and ADMIN_PASSWORD, compares password digests in constant time, and creates a random 256-bit opaque session token. The browser receives that token in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie; PostgreSQL stores only its hash, owner ID, and expiration. Every API replica consults the same session table. A browser-supplied owner field is never trusted, and a conversation query always includes both conversation ID and authenticated owner. An unknown or foreign conversation returns the same not-found response to avoid revealing its existence.

All modifying requests require an Origin header exactly matching APP_ORIGIN. This includes login, so cross-site login and cookie-based mutations encounter the same boundary. The sample cookie is deliberately configurable for local HTTP testing; set COOKIE_SECURE=true behind real HTTPS and set APP_ORIGIN to that exact public origin. HttpOnly prevents ordinary JavaScript from reading the cookie but does not neutralize script execution inside the application. The minimal client uses textContent to display model output rather than treating that output as HTML.

This is intentionally one shared demonstration account. Two people using Admin have the same owner and can access that owner's conversations if they possess their identifiers. It demonstrates the shape of authorization, not corporate identity isolation. Production work includes SSO integration, distinct immutable user IDs, account lifecycle handling, login throttling, session cleanup, revocation, audit policy, and appropriate password or identity-provider handling. A long ADMIN_PASSWORD does not substitute for those controls. The browser stores the conversation ID and an uncertain pending request locally; shared-device cleanup and retention requirements also need explicit treatment.

sections.title: 3. Reserve a turn in a short database transaction
paragraphs: A chat POST contains requestId, expectedRevision, text, and provider. The request ID is generated once by the browser and retained until the outcome becomes known. The server first obtains a row lock on the conversation. Within that short transaction it checks ownership, handles any expired generation, checks whether the request ID already exists, compares the expected revision, and rejects another running generation. Only then does it insert a turn containing the durable user text and an empty assistant field with running status. It increments the revision and commits before contacting inference.

PostgreSQL row locks prevent competing transactions from concurrently changing the same locked row until the transaction ends. In this application that supplies a serialization point for conversation decisions. A partial unique index also enforces at most one running turn per conversation. The transaction is not held open for token generation: doing so would consume a database connection and prolong lock contention throughout an unpredictable external operation. Database work ends before the fetch begins, while later fragment persistence uses short independent statements.

The revision is an optimistic concurrency guard for committed turn-state transitions. If two tabs both read revision 8 and submit different messages, the first accepted reservation advances it to 9; the second receives a conflict. It must reload the authoritative snapshot and let the user decide what to send next. Revisions advance again at terminal completion or stale-lease recovery, rather than once per text fragment. Therefore revision alone is not a stream offset and cannot indicate how many characters have arrived during a running turn.

sections.title: 4. Idempotency resolves ambiguity, not all execution duplication
paragraphs: A transport failure does not tell a browser whether its request reached the server. The reference fingerprints the text, selected provider, expected revision, and cloud-consent flag. Reusing a request ID with identical content returns the existing conversation snapshot; reusing it with different content is a conflict. The idempotency check precedes the revision check because a legitimate retry naturally carries the older revision that originally admitted the turn. This is why a client must not mint a fresh request ID whenever fetch throws.

The durable placeholder closes the dangerous gap in which inference could run without any database record of the attempted turn. It does not create an atomic transaction across PostgreSQL and an external model service. A process can commit a reservation and crash before sending the upstream request. It can also send the request and crash while the remote service continues computing. The application eventually records an interrupted outcome rather than automatically guessing that another execution is safe. The same request ID never starts a new inference after a reserved turn exists.

A retry of an active request returns a snapshot containing running status. The client polls the GET endpoint until it observes a terminal status, including lease-expiry recovery. This is snapshot reconciliation, not an SSE event replay log: missed transient events are not replayed by event ID. Persistent user text and assistant text are enough to restore the displayed conversation. Applications that require every token event, audit-grade delivery sequence, or resumable transport must add a durable event sequence and retention policy instead of implying that an HTTP stream supplies those properties.

sections.title: 5. Make the stream a projection of durable state
paragraphs: The gateway uses synchronous HTTP with server-sent event framing. The browser submits a POST with fetch and parses the response stream; native EventSource is not used because this operation needs a JSON request body. Events are separated by blank lines, and data lines are joined before JSON parsing. A network read is not necessarily a complete event: one read may contain half an event or several events. Both parsers retain an incomplete buffer and normalize the CRLF line endings encountered in typical providers.

The API emits accepted after reservation, delta for visible text, and snapshot after the terminal database commit. Before emitting each delta, it persists the accumulated assistant text using a conditional update that requires running status and an unexpired lease. This teaching implementation favors an understandable durability invariant over high throughput: anything displayed through a delta has already been saved. Writing the whole accumulated answer for every fragment is expensive and creates write amplification. A production variant would batch durable chunks and explicitly document whether the last displayed interval can be lost, or use an append-only event table.

The stream must end explicitly. OpenAI-compatible streams use their documented terminal convention; Claude emits message_stop. An EOF without the expected terminator is an interruption, even if text arrived. After an interruption with saved text the status becomes partial; without saved text it becomes error. Browser disconnection triggers best-effort cancellation and canceled status. The UI keeps these labels visible and excludes all non-complete turns from future prompt context, avoiding the accidental reuse of a truncated instruction or answer as a successful exchange. Complete means the provider stream terminated successfully, not that the answer is factually correct or necessarily satisfied the user's task. A provider may stop at its token limit and still terminate the transport normally; this scaffold does not save finish_reason or stop_reason, so complete can include a length-truncated answer. Production adapters should persist those reasons and show them in the client.

sections.title: 6. Recover crashes with a deadline and a fencing condition
paragraphs: The scaffold gives a turn a fixed 150-second database lease and places a 120-second total timeout around the gateway operation. A lease is a bounded claim to perform work; it is not a guarantee that a process remains alive or that an upstream server stops immediately. The additional interval leaves room for terminal persistence after a normal timeout. Each GET or chat reservation checks for expired running turns while holding the conversation lock. It changes an expired turn to partial if saved text exists, otherwise error, records lease_expired, and increments the revision.

Consider a turn reserved at 12:00:00. The API process crashes at 12:00:20 after saving 400 characters. A browser reconnects at 12:00:30 and sees running with that durable prefix. A later reconciliation after 12:02:30 marks the record partial. No second generation is silently launched. If the old process was merely paused and resumes, its next write includes both status=running and lease_until>now(); that update cannot overwrite the recovered terminal record. Conditional writes act as the fencing boundary, while the database clock decides expiry.

Recovery here is lazy rather than a continuously scanning worker. An abandoned conversation may remain labeled running in storage until its next read or write, although its expired lease prevents valid further writes. A scheduled sweeper would make operations dashboards converge without user activity. Long-running tasks need renewable leases, owner tokens, heartbeat policy, and careful fencing on every effect. If work must survive the loss of the requesting connection and resume automatically, switch to a durable job design with an outbox or work table, worker claims, and explicit retry semantics. Kafka alone supplies none of the conversation ordering or commit rules described here.
sections.formula: Generation timeout = 120 s; lease duration = 150 s; nominal finalization margin = 30 s. Margin is a design allowance, not a guarantee during database outage.

sections.title: 7. Route for locality without making locality a requirement
paragraphs: Nginx least_conn chooses an API replica based on active connection load. Because sessions and history live in PostgreSQL, that choice does not need to remain stable for a user. Express independently ranks the two inference nodes using a hash of conversation ID and stable node ID. The node with the highest hash score is preferred, subject to a short health check. This is rendezvous hashing: removing an unavailable node changes placement for keys that preferred it without requiring a shared placement table.

Locality is useful only when the serving configuration can exploit reusable prefixes. Consistently selecting node A does not guarantee a cache hit: competing requests, slot assignment, eviction, prompt formatting, and server restarts can destroy reuse. The full prompt is therefore rebuilt from PostgreSQL for every accepted turn. The same model identity on both servers includes weights, quantization, tokenizer, and template, not merely the string corp-qwen. Changing those independently can alter behavior even though transport and schemas still work.

The implementation probes candidates in rank order and can choose B if A fails its health check. A health check is a momentary observation; A can fail immediately afterward. This scaffold does not automatically retry an inference request on another node, even before text arrives, because an uncertain network error may conceal execution. After visible output begins, silent retry would be especially misleading: it can splice unrelated stochastic continuations into one answer or create unreported duplicate charges. A user may start an explicit new turn after reconciling the interrupted one, with the new attempt recorded separately.
sections.formula: preferred_node(c) = arg max over healthy nodes n of SHA256(conversation_id || stable_node_id). Hash scores rank placement; they do not measure load or authenticate a user.

sections.title: 8. Bound admission and context before the GPU becomes the queue
paragraphs: The sample permits four active chat handlers per Express process and returns 429 when that local bound is reached. With two API replicas, up to eight handlers can be admitted in aggregate. This is a protective demonstration bound, not a cluster-wide concurrency guarantee or an inference-slot scheduler. Uneven routing can reject requests at one replica while the other has free capacity. If each inference node has two decoding slots, eight admitted handlers can still exceed the four immediately executable slots and wait inside the serving layer.

A useful capacity calculation separates arrival rate from concurrency. At an illustrative arrival rate of 0.3 requests per second and a mean service time of 10 seconds, Little's-law concurrency is approximately three requests, assuming a stable system and consistent measurement boundaries. Doubling answer length might approximately double generation time in a decode-dominated workload, pushing average concurrency toward six before considering long-tail prompts. Those numbers are planning examples, not benchmark results. Measure time to first token, decode throughput, queue time, and request duration under the actual Qwen quantization and GPU configuration.

Input text is limited to 2,000 JavaScript characters per message, complete conversation context to 6,000 characters, and generated text to 16,000 characters with a requested 512-token output bound. Character limits bound application payloads but do not prove that a prompt fits the model context. Tokenization, chat-template overhead, Unicode, and provider-specific hidden tokens matter. The deployment uses an explicit context and slot configuration; a production gateway should count tokens with the matching tokenizer and reserve output capacity. This scaffold can still receive a context error, which becomes a visible failed turn rather than silent history truncation.
sections.formula: L = λW: requests = (requests/s) × s. Example: 0.3 × 10 = 3 mean in-flight requests; API admission cap = 2 replicas × 4 handlers = 8, not a measured sustainable rate.

sections.title: 9. Treat a cloud switch as a data-handling decision
paragraphs: The default provider is local. OpenAI or Claude requires ALLOW_CLOUD=true, a configured server-side key and model ID, and cloudConsent=true on that individual request. The UI explains that the completed history plus the new message will leave the local farm. A local outage never flips the provider automatically. These checks implement a simple consent gate, not a corporate data-loss-prevention system: classification, legal approval, regional restrictions, retention settings, and tenant-specific provider allowlists need separate policy enforcement before enterprise use.

The verified OpenAI adapter sends a streaming chat-completion request to https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions with bearer authentication, messages, model, and max_completion_tokens. The local llama.cpp adapter uses its OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions route and max_tokens. The Claude adapter sends to https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages with x-api-key, anthropic-version, messages, max_tokens, and stream. These are text-only adapters; tools, multimodal blocks, structured output, usage accounting, and reasoning events are intentionally outside their contract. Choose provider model IDs explicitly in the environment and verify their compatibility before running.

Provider APIs have different event schemas, even when the user-visible behavior is similar. The gateway extracts ordinary text deltas and maps failures into the same durable turn state. It does not claim the providers produce equivalent answers or share context limits. Request timeout and AbortController limit how long the gateway waits and request upstream cancellation when possible, but disconnecting cannot prove remote computation or billing stopped instantly. Keep provider keys exclusively server-side, avoid logging prompts by default, and record provider selection on each turn so later reconciliation preserves that decision.

sections.title: 10. Exercise the invariants, then state the limits honestly
paragraphs: Unpack the bundle, copy .env.example to .env, and follow the deployment README to set reachable inference URLs and real secrets. PostgreSQL initializes schema.sql on the first creation of its empty data volume. Subsequent schema changes require an explicit migration; editing the initialization file does not migrate an existing database. Start the control Compose project only after reviewing its Linux, Docker, model-path, and GPU prerequisites. Open the gateway at the configured origin, sign in, create a conversation, send a local message, and use Sync saved history to inspect the authoritative result.

Test correctness with adversarial sequences, not just a successful answer. Submit the same request ID twice with identical content and confirm only one turn is reserved. Change its text and expect a conflict. Open two tabs at the same revision and submit different requests; only one should be accepted. Cancel while text is streaming and verify that saved output remains visibly canceled. Stop an API process during a generation, wait beyond its lease, and reconcile through the other replica. The interrupted turn should become partial or error without automatic re-execution. Unavailable inference nodes should produce a recorded failure rather than an untracked user message.

The reference passed server and client syntax checks, fragmented UTF-8/CRLF/multiline SSE parsing tests, EOF and frame-size tests, and article structure validation during authoring; no live PostgreSQL, Docker, GPU, or paid-provider integration run is claimed. Before production, add representative integration tests for these sequences, dependency locking and scanning, global admission or fairness, shared login rate limiting beyond the process-wide 20-attempts-per-minute sample throttle, request metrics, structured error classification, retention and deletion, backup recovery, schema migrations, and secure deployment. The parser targets ordinary text SSE rather than every optional protocol feature. Its slow-client strategy aborts when response buffering exceeds Node's writable threshold instead of maintaining an unbounded queue. These limits keep the example reviewable while making the system's central consistency rules concrete.

interview.question: Two API replicas serve a conversation. The client saw half an answer, its connection dropped, and it retries through the other replica. Explain the exact state transitions and why neither sticky sessions nor Kafka solves this alone.
interview.answer: The original transaction reserved the user text and running assistant under a conversation lock, incrementing the revision before inference. Each displayed fragment was persisted first. A retry carries the original request ID and fingerprint, so the second replica returns existing state instead of starting another generation; it checks idempotency before comparing the stale expected revision. GET reconciliation restores persisted text. If the original process survives it records canceled or another terminal outcome. If it died, a read after the fixed lease marks the saved prefix partial, or error if empty, and advances revision. Conditional writes fence an expired writer. Sticky routing can improve cache locality but supplies no durable authority; a queue would still need reservation, ownership, leases, ordering, and terminal-state rules. There is no claim of exactly-once remote model execution.
followUps: How would you batch token persistence while describing the maximum text-loss window honestly?
How would a renewable lease with an owner epoch prevent an old worker from committing?
Where would you enforce tenant fairness and a global inference-slot budget?
How would you support an explicit retry that preserves both the failed attempt and the new result?

pitfalls: Using a browser-provided owner ID or hashing a bearer token as the routing key.
Holding a PostgreSQL transaction open throughout inference.
Generating a new idempotency key for every network retry.
Calling an interrupted answer complete because the socket reached EOF.
Assuming fixed node affinity guarantees a prefix-cache hit.
Treating replica-local admission as a global GPU capacity controller.
Exporting local history to cloud as an invisible outage fallback.
Equating character limits with verified model token limits.
Treating the single shared Admin demonstration account as multi-user enterprise authorization.
checklist: Verify ownership on both chat and snapshot routes.
Commit user text and reserved assistant before contacting inference.
Check duplicate request fingerprints before expected revisions.
Release the database connection before the external call.
Fence every text and terminal write with running status and lease validity.
Preserve partial/error/canceled labels and reconcile from saved state.
Keep endpoints and provider keys server-side; require explicit cloud policy and consent.
Test crashes, duplicate requests, stale tabs, slow clients, and context overflow against real infrastructure before deployment.

flashcards.front: Which component owns conversation truth in the farm?
flashcards.back: PostgreSQL, with Express enforcing its write rules. Inference caches are disposable and cannot provide durable ownership, turn ordering, or recovery.
A random cookie resolves to a live database session rather than allowing the browser to choose an identity. Every replica can authenticate it, and conversation ownership is checked separately.

flashcards.front: What belongs inside the conversation reservation transaction?
flashcards.back: Ownership, duplicate detection, revision and active-turn checks, user/assistant reservation, and revision advancement. Inference stays outside because a long external call must not hold database locks or connections.

flashcards.front: Why check idempotency before the expected revision?
flashcards.back: A legitimate retry carries the revision used before its original reservation advanced state. Returning the existing request resolves uncertainty without rejecting a valid retry or generating another answer.

flashcards.front: What happens when a request ID is reused with changed text?
flashcards.back: The stored fingerprint differs and the gateway returns a conflict. An idempotency key identifies one immutable logical attempt, not permission to overwrite it.
A displayed delta has already reached the database, so reconnecting can recover it. It increases write load; batching changes the possible loss window and must be disclosed.

flashcards.front: Why is EOF insufficient to call an answer complete?
flashcards.back: A broken connection can end without the provider's terminal event. Saved output then becomes partial, while an empty failed answer becomes error, preserving honest semantics.

flashcards.front: How does the fixed lease recover a crashed generation?
flashcards.back: A later read or write finds an expired running record and marks it partial or error. Conditional writes require a valid lease and running status, preventing a late process from overwriting recovery.

flashcards.front: Does the example replay missed SSE events?
flashcards.back: No. It returns an authoritative snapshot with durable text and status. Exact event replay would need durable sequence numbers and a retained event log.
It ranks same-model nodes consistently by conversation and node ID, creating possible prefix locality. It neither authenticates callers nor guarantees cache hits or balanced live load.

flashcards.front: Why avoid silent retry after tokens are visible?
flashcards.back: A second stochastic execution can diverge, duplicate computation, and make the shown prefix inconsistent with the continuation. Record the interrupted attempt and require an explicit new action.

flashcards.front: Why is a four-request per-process cap not a farm-wide cap?
flashcards.back: Two replicas can admit eight combined requests, and placement may be uneven. Global capacity and tenant fairness require coordination beyond a process-local counter.

flashcards.front: What authorizes a cloud switch in the reference?
flashcards.back: Operator enablement, configured credentials/model, explicit selected provider, and per-request consent. A local failure never supplies permission to export completed history.

flashcards.front: Why do bounded characters not prove context fits?
flashcards.back: Token counts vary with language, tokenizer, template, and provider behavior. Exact budgeting requires the matching tokenizer plus reserved output and template overhead; context errors must remain visible.
